newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis reaches dangerous deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis reaches dangerous deadlock.

text.p: Peru's 19-day hostage crisis drifted into a difficult and dangerous impasse at the weekend, with contact between the government and Marxist rebels hanging by a thread and the release of hostages paralysed.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo had not spoken to the rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) for a week by Sunday, and after some hints of flexibility before the New Year, both sides have entrenched themselves in their original uncompromising positions.
The rebels want some 400 imprisoned comrades freed, but the government has flatly refused their main demand.

"The process of dialogue between the MRTA and the government of President Alberto Fujimori has become bogged down, and there is no immediate solution," said opposition legislator Maximo San Roman Caceres, a former Peruvian vice president under Fujimori.
He suggested that the Pope mediate in the stand-off.

With Palermo, Fujimori's education minister, staying away from the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador stormed by the guerrillas on Dec. 17, the only lines of communication were through the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Roman Catholic church.
"It is obviously not easy, and it will not be quick, to reconcile the two sides," Red Cross spokesman Ronald Bigler told Reuters. "Patience is a good counsellor."
As the stand-off entered its fourth straight day with no new release of hostages, some commentators were concerned the government might turn to the option of using force.
Police sources said last week a plan to storm the residence was ready and training by special assault units complete.

"The only thing that so far appears to have stopped things getting worse...(is) the contact established between the government and the MRTA hostage takers," commentator Juan Paredes Castro wrote in El Comercio newspaper.
"One of the signs of its being in effect and making progress is the yardstick of releases obtained."
The rebels were still holding 74 hostages on Sunday, and none had been let go since New Year's Day -- the longest period without a release of captives since the siege began.

Dialogue with the rebels "is the path that works as long as the terrorist organisation does not bring the government to use the other path, under consideration from the start: the use of force," Paredes wrote.
The rebels have freed some 430 of their original captives.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said the reduction in hostage numbers made things harder rather than easier to resolve, though.
"The number of hostages has been reduced to a level where it is easier for the terrorists to control them," he told reporters on Saturday.
Roman Catholic Bishop Luis Cipriani, a close personal friend of Fujimori, was the other go-between entering the residence on a regular basis, ostensibly to lend spiritual support to the hostages.
His closeness to Fujimori has led some commentators to suggest that he is maintaining a line, albeit tenuous, open to the rebels.
"Direct talks cannot always be carried out in public," Bigler said when asked about such suggestions, but he declined to elaborate.
